fact: Jordan Belfort was inspired to write his memoir, which became the basis for the film, by his prison cellmate, Tommy Chong.
short: The film's memoir was inspired by actor Tommy Chong, the protagonist's prison cellmate.
long: While serving time in a Californian prison, the real-life stockbroker Jordan Belfort shared stories of his Wall Street career with Chong, who then encouraged him to write them down.

fact: The prop cocaine snorted by actors was actually crushed-up Vitamin B, which led to Jonah Hill contracting bronchitis and requiring hospitalization due to inhaling so much.
short: Jonah Hill was hospitalized after snorting prop cocaine for the film.
long: The actor developed bronchitis for three weeks after snorting vitamin powder daily for seven months during production.

fact: The real Donnie Azoff, whose actual name is Danny Porush, truly did swallow a goldfish, as depicted in the film.
short: The real co-founder who inspired Jonah Hill's character actually ate a live goldfish.
long: The real Danny Porush, who inspired Jonah Hill's character Donnie Azoff, confessed to eating a broker's goldfish, recalling he threatened, "If you don't do more business, I'm gonna eat your goldfish!" before doing it.

fact: During the fight scene between Brad and Donnie, actor Jon Bernthal accidentally punched Jonah Hill, causing Hill's prosthetic teeth to break and fly out, but director Martin Scorsese kept filming to capture Hill's reaction.
short: Jonah Hill's prosthetic teeth broke when co-star Jon Bernthal accidentally punched him.
long: During the fight scene, actor Jon Bernthal accidentally landed a real punch on Jonah Hill, causing Hill's prosthetic teeth to split and fall out, which director Martin Scorsese kept filming.

fact: The "sell me this pen" scene was improvised by Leonardo DiCaprio, who got the idea from a story his security guard had heard from the real Jordan Belfort.
short: Leonardo DiCaprio improvised the lead's iconic "sell me this pen" scene.
long: The idea for the scene came from a story Leonardo DiCaprio's security guard shared about a job interview with the real Jordan Belfort, where he was asked to sell a pen.

fact: The iconic chest-thumping and humming ritual performed by Mark Hanna was Matthew McConaughey's own pre-scene preparation, and Leonardo DiCaprio suggested incorporating it into the film.
short: Matthew McConaughey's chest-thumping ritual was his own prep, added by Leonardo DiCaprio.
long: The actor used the chest-thumping and humming as a relaxation tool for years, and his co-star Leonardo DiCaprio suggested adding it to the scene after observing him.

fact: Margot Robbie insisted on performing her nude scene without a bathrobe, believing it suited Naomi's character to use her body as a weapon.
short: Naomi's actor, Margot Robbie, insisted on full nudity for a scene.
long: Robbie believed her character's body was her "only form of currency" in the film's world. She insisted on appearing fully nude to show Naomi "laying her cards on the table," rejecting an initial plan for her to wear a robe.

fact: During Jordan and Naomi's first sex scene, the dog refused to jump on the bed, requiring filmmakers to put dog food and chicken livers on Leonardo DiCaprio's feet and between his toes to coax it.
short: Leonardo DiCaprio's feet were covered in dog food for the dog scene.
long: The dog in the scene initially refused to jump on the bed, so the crew spread a smelly paste of dog food and chicken livers on the lead actor's feet, making the small set hot and smelly.

fact: Jonah Hill passionately argued with Leonardo DiCaprio about why he should play Donnie Azoff, leading DiCaprio to recommend him to Martin Scorsese, who then hired Hill on the spot.
short: Jonah Hill's impassioned pitch to Leonardo DiCaprio led to his on-the-spot casting as Donnie Azoff.
long: Jonah Hill was so determined to play the character Donnie Azoff that he passionately argued with Leonardo DiCaprio, who then immediately recommended him to director Martin Scorsese, leading to Hill's on-the-spot hiring.

fact: The role of Aunt Emma, played by Joanna Lumley, was initially offered to Julie Andrews, who declined due to recovering from an ankle injury.
short: Julie Andrews declined Aunt Emma's role due to post-surgery medication.
long: Actress Julie Andrews was offered the role of Aunt Emma but declined due to recovering from an operation for a titanium ankle, which left her heavily affected by anesthetics and pain medication. Joanna Lumley ultimately played the part.

fact: Margot Robbie took three shots of tequila to relax before shooting her nude scene.
short: The lead's wife, Margot Robbie, took tequila shots to calm her nerves before filming her nude scene.
long: The actress, who was 22 at the time, confessed she was "very, very nervous" about the intimate scene, which was her first nude performance.

fact: The fake paper bills used in the sex scene on a bed of cash had sharp edges, causing multiple cuts on both Margot Robbie and Leonardo DiCaprio.
short: The fake money in the love scene gave lead actress Margot Robbie 'a million paper cuts'.
long: The fake money used in the intimate scene was so sharp that Margot Robbie, who plays the lead's second wife, came away with numerous red marks, prompting the crew to say she looked 'whipped a million times'.

fact: Before Martin Scorsese directed, Ridley Scott was reportedly interested in directing "The Wolf of Wall Street" with Brad Pitt considered for the role of Jordan Belfort.
short: Brad Pitt was almost the lead, Jordan Belfort, with Ridley Scott directing.
long: Brad Pitt was considered to play the lead, Jordan Belfort, with Ridley Scott directing. However, Scott's commitment to direct 'Prometheus' ultimately put the film on hold, leading to Martin Scorsese taking over.

fact: The meeting with the private detective was filmed at the legendary Rao's restaurant in East Harlem, a Southern Italian establishment founded in 1896, which played itself in the film and is known for being one of America's hardest reservations.
short: The restaurant in this scene is the real Rao's, a Southern Italian spot founded in 1896.
long: This legendary Southern Italian restaurant, located in East Harlem, served as the filming location for the private investigator's meeting with the protagonist.

fact: Giorgio Armani collaborated with costume designers, creating initial sketches and designing two pinstripe suits for Leonardo DiCaprio's Jordan Belfort, aiming to capture the era's "power dressing" style.
short: Fashion icon Giorgio Armani designed the pinstripe suits worn by the film's lead, Jordan Belfort.
long: Armani created initial sketches with the costume designers, defining how Leonardo DiCaprio would bring the character to life on screen, including both navy and grey pinstripe options.

fact: Martin Scorsese provides the voice for the first client Jordan Belfort sells penny stocks to, a man named John.
short: Director Martin Scorsese has a voice cameo as the first client the lead sells to.
long: Director Martin Scorsese lends his voice to John, the first person the lead character, Jordan, sells Aerotyne I.N.D. penny stocks to.

fact: Nadine Macaluso, the real-life Naomi Lapaglia, stated in a podcast that the film was approximately 90% accurate in depicting their chaotic life, including events like a boat sinking and a plane crash.
short: Nadine Macaluso found the film accurate from Jordan Belfort's view, but not her own.
long: Nadine Macaluso, the real-life inspiration for Margot Robbie's character, claimed the film was mainly accurate from Jordan Belfort's perspective. However, she clarified that the film's depiction was not accurate from her own point of view regarding their marriage.

fact: The initial assembly cut of the film was four hours long, but director Martin Scorsese, who rarely releases director's cuts, did not include this longer version on the Blu-ray/DVD release.
short: The Wolf of Wall Street's first cut was four hours, but director Martin Scorsese never released it.
long: This extended version was trimmed down from the assembly cut to meet studio distribution demands, which capped the final film at three hours. Director Martin Scorsese considers the theatrical release the definitive version, stating he doesn't believe in "director's cuts."

fact: Actress Reese Witherspoon had a clause in her contract that allowed her to keep all of the lead character, Elle Woods', outfits from the film.
short: Actress Reese Witherspoon had a contract clause to keep all of Elle Woods' outfits.
long: The lead actress, Reese Witherspoon, had a contract clause to keep all of Elle Woods' outfits, including 77 pairs of Jimmy Choo shoes.

fact: The author's original manuscript for the novel was famously written on pink paper, a detail referenced in the film through the lead character's scented pink résumés.
short: The novel's author famously wrote her manuscript on pink paper, inspiring the lead's pink résumés.
long: This distinctive choice helped the author's manuscript stand out to an agent, a detail later mirrored by the lead character's memorable scented pink résumés in the film.

fact: The initial script for the film was much raunchier, similar to American Pie, and did not feature the murder trial, instead ending with the lead character, Elle, in a relationship with a professor.
short: The film's initial script was much raunchier, similar to American Pie, and the lead dated a professor.
long: The original script was described as "very raunchy" and "in the vein of American Pie," and it didn't feature the murder trial, instead concluding with the protagonist in a relationship with a professor.

fact: The actor playing Warner Huntington III had a real-life crush on the lead actress since he was 15 and was so nervous acting with her that producers had to intervene.
short: The actor playing Warner Huntington III was so nervous around Reese Witherspoon that producers intervened.
long: Matthew Davis, who played Warner Huntington III, had harbored a crush on Reese Witherspoon since he was 15, causing him to act like a "bumbling idiot" on set and prompting producers to check on him.

fact: The iconic pink satin bunny ears lingerie worn by the lead character was sourced and created in the stockroom of an intimates shop called Trashy Lingerie.
short: The lead's iconic pink bunny costume was created in an intimates shop's stockroom.
long: Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff had the famous ensemble built and fitted for the lead at Trashy Lingerie on La Cienega.

fact: The scene where the lead character picks up her class schedule and asks for social events at 'Harvard' was actually filmed on the flagstone patio of UCLA's Kerckhoff Hall.
short: Elle's 'Harvard' class schedule pickup was filmed at UCLA's Kerckhoff Hall.
long: The patio of UCLA's Kerckhoff Hall stood in for Harvard Law School in the scene where the lead character, Elle, picks up her class schedule and asks for social events. UCLA often serves as a stand-in for Harvard in films because Harvard generally doesn’t allow commercial filming on its campus.

fact: The production designer deliberately designed the lead character's sorority house in a colorful California mission style, contrasting it with her Harvard dorm, which featured a muted palette based on actual Harvard dorms.
short: The production designer intentionally contrasted the lead's colorful sorority house with her muted Harvard dorm.
long: Production designer Missy Stewart created distinct mood boards for the lead's California sorority house, filling it with striking pinks, greens, and a leafy atmosphere, then toned down the palette for her Harvard dorm.

fact: The lead character's Porsche had a personalized license plate that read '22BLONDE'.
short: The lead character's convertible sported a vanity license plate reading '22BLONDE'.
long: The personalized California license plate, which read '22BLONDE', was a screen-used prop seen on the lead character Elle Woods' convertible.

fact: The lead character's head-to-toe pink courtroom dress was a deliberate costume choice by designer Sophie de Rakoff to show her being her 'most true self' and to subvert stereotypes.
short: Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff chose the lead's pink courtroom dress to show her 'most true self'.
long: The head-to-toe pink outfit was meant to deliberately upend social expectations, turning a 'girly' color into a statement of female power and confidence for the lead character.

fact: An early alternate ending for the film showed the lead character, Elle, and Vivian in Hawaii, drinking margaritas and holding hands, with the insinuation they were either best friends or romantically involved.
short: An early alternate ending for the film showed the lead, Elle, and Vivian in Hawaii, hinting at romance.
long: Actresses Jessica Cauffiel and Alanna Ubach recalled this ending, where the two characters were drinking margaritas and holding hands, but the film's screenwriters deny writing it.

fact: The lead character, Elle Woods', LSAT score was 179, just one point shy of a perfect score of 180, indicating her exceptional intelligence.
short: The lead character, Elle Woods, scored a near-perfect 179 on her LSAT.
long: The lead character, Elle Woods, scored a near-perfect 179 on her LSAT, just one point shy of the maximum 180, a remarkable jump from her initial practice score of 143.
